content.section: 6.1.3 Patient selection for implantable cardioverter-defibrillator therapy
points: Patients with HFrEF and QRS duration ≥130 ms can be considered for CRT with a defibrillator (CRT‑D) rather than ICD; see CRT section for details.

ICD therapy is not recommended in patients in NYHA class IV with severe symptoms refractory to pharmacological therapy who are not candidates for VAD or cardiac transplantation (limited life expectancy; likely to die from pump failure).
Patients with serious comorbidities unlikely to survive >1 year with good quality of life are unlikely to obtain substantial benefit from an ICD.

DANISH trial did not show significant benefit from ICD in NICM overall; however NICM is heterogeneous and subgroups (e.g., laminopathies, sarcoidosis) are at higher risk of sudden death and may merit careful consideration for ICD implantation.
Tools to help risk stratification (e.g., scar burden on MRI) can be helpful.

Patients should be counselled about purpose, complications, implications for driving, risk of inappropriate shocks, and circumstances under which defibrillator/CRT‑D component might be deactivated or explanted (terminal disease, infection, recovery of LV function).
Shared decision making recommended when ICD generator reaches end of life or requires explantation; careful evaluation by experienced cardiologist as treatment goals may have changed.
Controversy exists whether patients whose LVEF has greatly improved and who have not required device therapy during ICD lifetime should receive another device.
section_6.1.4_points: Routine defibrillation threshold testing is no longer performed after ICD or CRT‑D implantation as it does not improve shock efficacy or reduce arrhythmic death.
Conservative programming with long delays between detection and therapy delivery reduces risk of inappropriate and unnecessary shocks.
For primary prevention, defibrillators are generally programmed to minimize pacing (e.g., VVI at 40/min) and to have a tachycardia treatment zone >200/min.
Programming should be adapted to patient’s specific needs, particularly for secondary prevention.
section_6.1.5_points: Subcutaneous ICDs (S‑ICDs) appear as effective as transvenous ICDs with similar complication rates; early higher risk of inappropriate shocks improved with better patient selection.
S‑ICDs are non‑inferior to transvenous ICDs in some analyses and may be preferred for patients with difficult venous access or those requiring ICD explantation due to infection.
S‑ICDs cannot treat bradyarrhythmia (except post‑shock pacing), cannot deliver anti‑tachycardia pacing or CRT; careful patient selection required.
Substantial randomized trial data and long‑term safety/efficacy data are still awaited.
